title: For Whom and What We Are to Pray
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Scope of Intercession: The Whole Church
subpoints: Prayer for the universal body of Christ, not just local congregations
The Second Petition of the Lord's Prayer ('Your kingdom come') as a command for corporate prayer
The necessity of being informed about the global church to pray effectively

outline.title: Prayer for Magistrates and Ministers
subpoints: Direct command in 1 Timothy 2 to pray for kings and those in authority
Prayer as a means to secure a quiet and peaceable life
Requesting wisdom, integrity, and the opening of doors for the ministry of the Word

outline.title: Prayer for Oneself
subpoints: Legitimacy of praying for temporal and spiritual needs
The necessity of submitting requests to God's will ('Your will be done')

outline.title: Prayer for Brethren
subpoints: Corporate responsibility to pray for the unity and growth of fellow believers
Examples of apostolic intercession in the Epistles

outline.title: Prayer for Enemies
subpoints: The command to bless and pray for persecutors
The inevitability of conflict in a fallen world and the Christian response

summary:
In this Sunday school session, Pastor Tito Lyro continues the series on the Westminster Larger Catechism, focusing on Questions 183 and 184 regarding the subjects and content of Christian prayer. The teaching emphasizes that prayer is not merely a personal habit but a Trinitarian act that must align with the priorities established in Scripture. The primary focus is on identifying 'whom' we are to pray for, correcting common misconceptions that often prioritize unsaved family members over biblically mandated groups.

The sermon outlines five key categories for intercession: the whole church of Christ, magistrates and ministers, oneself, brethren, and enemies. It highlights the direct command in 1 Timothy 2 to pray for civil leaders, noting that such prayers are essential for a godly and peaceable life. Furthermore, it addresses the tension between praying for personal needs and maintaining a selfless attitude, urging believers to submit their requests to God's sovereign will.

Finally, the session addresses the challenging command to pray for enemies. It clarifies that this involves blessing and seeking their good, rather than cursing or seeking their destruction. By aligning the scope of prayer with biblical instruction, believers are called to reflect the heart of Christ in their intercessions, covering the global church, societal authorities, and even those who oppose them.
